Alabama Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Cash Home Buyers in Alabama

Selling a Alabama House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Alabama statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Alabama law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Adverse possession cannot confer or defeat title to land unless the claimant shows one of three things: (1) a deed or other color of title recorded with the county probate judge for 10 years before the action; (2) he and those through whom he claims annually listed the land for taxation for 10 years before the action, if the land is taxable; or (3) he derives title by descent cast or devise from a predecessor in title who was in possession. (Ala. Code § 6-5-200(a); source)
  • Recorded color-of-title periods of the claimant and those through whom he claims may be added together to reach 10 years; an inadvertent failure to list the land for taxation or an unintentional assessment mistake during the 10 years does not bar the claim. (Ala. Code § 6-5-200(b); source)
  • The Code of Alabama contains a separate Chapter 9B titled 'Squatting' (§§ 35-9B-1 to 35-9B-9) in Title 35, Property. (Ala. Code Title 35, Ch. 9B (table of contents); source)
  • A landlord may bring an action for possession against a tenant who remains in possession without consent after the term expires or the lease is terminated; a willful holdover allows recovery of up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-441(c); source)
Selling in Alabama?
We buy Alabama houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated here. Read the statute sections linked above for the full text, and confirm deadlines with the court or county office.

How to sell a Alabama house when this applies to you

  1. Write down who is in the house and on what terms: owner, heirs, tenants or occupants with no lease.
  2. Ask the title company what it needs to insure the sale, such as a recorded deed, court papers or a payoff letter.
  3. Get the payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the proceeds at closing.
  4. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. See we buy houses in Alabama.

What a cash sale of a Alabama house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Alabama.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Alabama disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Alabama

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Alabama change, so confirm details with the official office or a Alabama attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Alabama

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Alabama Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Alabama house?

Only by meeting every requirement of the adverse possession statute cited above for the full period. Check the statute and talk to a Alabama attorney about your facts.

Can I sell a house that has squatters in it?

Yes. We buy houses as-is, including occupied ones. Tell us who is in the property when you request an offer.

Should I remove a squatter myself?

No. Use the legal process described in the official sources above. Self-help removal can create liability for the owner.

Alabama statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit may not exceed one month's periodic rent, except for pets, changes to the premises, or increased liability risks. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-201(a); source)
  • Landlord must refund the deposit or deliver an itemized list of deductions within 60 days after termination of the tenancy and delivery of possession; the tenant must give a written forwarding address; if the landlord fails to mail a timely refund or accounting, the landlord owes double the original deposit. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-201(b)-(f); source)
  • A month-to-month tenancy may be ended by either party with written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice; week-to-week requires 7 days. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-441(a)-(b); source)
  • Landlord entry: at least two days' notice, at reasonable times; posting a note on the primary door is a permitted method of notice; entry without consent allowed in an emergency, by court order, or on reasonable belief of abandonment. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-303(b)-(c); source)
  • Retaliation: a landlord may not retaliate by discriminatorily increasing rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession because the tenant complained to a code agency, complained of a 35-9A-204 violation, or joined a tenants' union; exceptions include tenant default in rent and other material lease violations. Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Alabama
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Alabama statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Alabama law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: landlord may deliver written notice stating the rent and late fees owed; lease terminates if not remedied within seven business days after receipt. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-421(b); source)
  • Material lease violation (or health/safety noncompliance under 35-9A-301): written notice with termination date not less than seven business days after receipt; tenant may cure before that date; an intentional material misrepresentation in the lease or application may not be cured. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-421(a); source)
  • No lease breach may be cured more than two times in a 12-month period without landlord's written consent; certain noncurable defaults (illegal drugs, illegal firearm use, criminal assault, repeat same breach within six months) allow termination on seven-day notice. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-421(d); source)
  • No-cause end of month-to-month tenancy: written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-441(b); source)
  • After the term ends or the lease is terminated, a holdover tenant may be sued for possession by the landlord. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-441(c); source)
